blocks.text: Witness statement of MS AMY DAVIES (read)

My Lord, may I begin by reading some statements that we intended to read last week before circumstances caused us to have to adjourn. It's a statement of Amy Davies at page 27 of the first of two reading bundles that your Lordship has received.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Amy Davies made a statement dated 23 May 2018 regarding her involvement with a set of triplets born on 21 June 2016 at the Countess of Chester Hospital:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At the specified time I was working as a neonatal practitioner. I recall [Baby O], [Baby P] and [Baby R], and although I did not have any involvement in their care when they were first born, it was during the night of 21 June 2016 that I looked after both babies.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was working a night shift on 21 June 2016 and I was the designated nurse for [Baby O] and [Baby P]. During the handover I cannot recall any concerns or issues raised by the day staff. The care that I provided during that shift was very straightforward. Both babies were on CPAP and there were no concerns.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When a baby is on CPAP, they obviously need that additional support, which makes them vulnerable, but I had no concerns about them. I have confirmed this by reviewing the notes made at that time, which also documents the babies were on antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I confirm that my initials AD are present at the bottom of the observation charts. Within [Baby P]'s notes I have documented that his cannula tissued during the night so it stopped working and this caused his arm to become swollen. As a result, the cannula was replaced with another and the replacement was uneventful. This is quite a common occurrence and I had detailed that it was a doctor who replaced the cannula.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Both babies had blood gases to check that they were stable and the results confirmed they were. The triplets' parents visited and I updated them in relation to both [Baby O] and [Baby P] and I think the parents then returned to the ward for the night and I didn't see them again after that.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I recall that [Mother of Babies O, P & R] was still in a wheelchair and recovering from her caesarean. I was happy with both babies during that night shift and I believe that they remained in nursery 1. From what I can remember, [Baby R] was in nursery 2, although I had no involvement with [Baby R] and I didn't look after the triplets again following that shift.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I would have ended my night shift at 08.00 hours on the morning of the 22 June 2016, but I am unsure of the member of staff I handed over to.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I worked the following night shift on 22 June 2016, but I did not look after any of the [Surname of Babies O, P & R] triplets. I am unsure of when I next worked a shift at the Countess of Chester Hospital as I only work three shifts a week, but I believe it was after [Baby O] and [Baby P] had passed away."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS CAROLINE OAKLEY (read)
The next statement to be read is at page 30, my Lord, a statement made by Caroline Oakley on 31 July 2018, which reads:

blocks.text: "From accessing the computer system, Meditech, within the hospital, I can see that I worked a night shift on the 21st and 22 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 21 June, the day the triplets were born, I came on duty at 19.30 hours. I was shift leader that night and I really cannot remember anything about them. blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "His parents had visited some time during the shift. [Baby P] was also looked after by Amy on 21 June. He was also on CPAP and he was fine and stable. I don't remember anything else specific about that shift and the [Surname of Babies O, P & R] triplets.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 22 June, I was the shift leader again coming on shift at 19.30 hours. I was in charge on the shift and I was working with Amy Davies, Sophie Ellis, Nicky Dennison and Val Thomas. [Baby O] was being looked after by Sophie Ellis on 22 June and he had obviously done quite well in the day as on the night shift he had come down from CPAP to Optiflow, which is less respiratory
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: support. He was still on intravenous fluids, but had started to take a little bit of milk. This will have probably been just a tube up his nose and into his tummy.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "His antibiotics had stopped at 36 hours, so obviously he was clinically well, and his blood results were okay. I have made a note towards the end of the shift that his abdomen became distended and he was reviewed by Dr Mayberry and he said that clinically he seemed okay, so just carry on and monitor. I assume the request was made to Dr Mayberry by Sophie Ellis and she will have updated me as well, as I was in charge of the shift that night.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby P] was also being looked at on 22 June by Sophie Ellis. He had obviously had a good day shift because he had also gone down from CPAP to Optiflow (inaudible) some intravenous fluids and also started some feeds. His antibiotics had stopped and his blood results were okay. So overnight from 22 June into 23 June, both [Baby O] and [Baby P] were progressing well.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "For the night shift of 22 June, I was not the designated nurse for any of the triplets; I was the shift leader. So at the end of the shift on the morning of 23 June 2016, I would hand over to the morning staff and there was nothing of concern to comment on. [Baby O] did have a full tummy. Obviously it was enough of a concern for us to ask the doctor to conduct a review. There was nothing with [Baby P] but we also thought [Baby R]'s tummy was full so we also requested a review on him.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "So obviously, there was something with the two with the tummies. I did not work the shifts on the 23rd and 24 June 2016 at all. By the time I returned to work, sadly both [Baby O] and [Baby P] had passed away. There is no further information I can provide in relation to the [Surname of Babies O, P & R] triplets."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS VICKY BLAMIRE (read)
Finally, my Lord, at this stage, may I read a statement from a Vicky Blamire. It's at page 34 of the bundle and it's dated 26 January 2018 and it reads:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have been asked with reference to the care of [Baby O] and in particular 22/23 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I recall [Baby O] as he was one of three triplets who all appeared to be doing well. I was working a night shift on the 22nd into 23 June 2016 and it was a busy night shift. blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I went into nursery 2 and no other members of staff were present. As I approached [Baby O]'s cot, I could see everything I needed for the feed was laid out ready. blocks.text: "To feed the child, you can either filter the milk from the syringe through the nasal tube into the stomach or place the milk on to a stand within the incubator and gravity will then feed it through the tube and into the baby's stomach.

blocks.text: "I noticed that [Baby O]'s stomach was distended (swollen) and told Sophie this. She told me that she was aware and had asked for a review by the paediatric doctor, but had been told to go ahead with the feed but closely monitor the stomach.

blocks.text: "I fed [Baby O] and remember him squirming a little as he was being fed. I will have signed for this tube feed on the feeding charts, which are kept on the end of the cots. blocks.text: Yvonne Rose Farmer, in a statement dated 13 March 2018, says this. I should describe, she is a nurse by profession. We have edited the statement down:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On 22 June 2016, I was working a long day clinical shift on the unit, which had commenced at 07.30 hours. I recall looking after [Baby P] on this date and I think I also looked after one other patient.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby P] was in nursery 2. We call this our high dependency room and we have access to all the gases and equipment. During that afternoon, I remember one of my colleagues moving [Baby P]'s brother [Baby O] from nursery 1 to nursery 2. I recall this as nursery 1 was busy and, due to limited available bed spaces, we had to move babies around.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I believe my colleague Sam O'Brien was [Baby O]'s designated nurse that shift and I supported her in moving [Baby O] whilst Sam was caring for another baby in nursery 1. [Baby O] needed a new IV site as well. I also assisted with [Baby O]'s drip and intravenous fluids whilst the cannulation procedure was conducted.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We do share our workload and as a team we help each other where we can. My involvement has been documented by Sam and is visible within the nurses' records. I also recall that [Baby O] had been on nasal CPAP and had been downgraded to high flow. The [Surname of Babies O, P & R] babies were quite difficult to cannulate as their peripheral circulations were quite poor. This is common in premature babies but it is all dependent on the individual baby. From reading the notes, I can see that all three of the triplets had problems with their IV access.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On 23 June 2016, I was working an 08.00 to 17.00 hours day shift and in a practice development role. Some time towards the afternoon, I was inside the office when I was alerted to [Baby O]'s collapse. I am unsure who made me aware of the situation, but [Baby O] was in nursery 2 and was quickly transferred back to nursery 1.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We make this decision as nursery 1 is a larger room and allows more staff to be involved and provides increased access to the
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: babies. It also makes it easier in the event of a transport team assisting with the transferring-out of a baby.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I made my way to nursery 1. As I entered nursery 1, I saw Lucy Letby, [Dr A] and [Nurse C]. I am unsure of whether any other colleagues were present. [Baby O] was being intubated and I cannot confirm whether I was involved in administering drugs but I was present in a support role.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Any baby requiring resuscitation has cardiac massage and another member of staff manages their airway. Two more people are required to draw up and check the drugs and to document the drugs administered. We have a written resuscitation drug pro forma so we know exactly the amount of drugs to give to the baby and in which order. We document the time we start resuscitation and the time we start cardiac massage. This results in an accurate record of the procedure.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The drugs are already in nursery 1 and we have a resuscitation trolley. On top of the trolley, or by the trolley, there is a sealed box containing all of the drugs needed along with the pro forma. All the items are within easy reach and these are kept separately from all the other drugs. Once the seal is broken, the drugs are in a set order. This negates having to search for the drugs required or having to leave the room. Once the box has been used for a baby, the box is returned to the pharmacy and is either destroyed or a new box is made up.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We draw up the drugs. This involves two members of staff and we hand the drugs to our colleagues conducting the resuscitation. I don't know if it would have been Lucy or one of the doctors who administered the drugs to [Baby O]. With any resuscitation, a consultant is called and we ended up with three consultants present that shift. I know I stayed at the unit until approximately 17.30 hours. My colleague Yvonne Griffiths was still on the unit and she took over from me and I am aware that it was soon after I left that [Baby O] passed way.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I do recall Dr Gibbs and [Dr B] both being in the room. It is possible that this is when I was called into the room as I do recall scribing at one point, but I cannot say for certain.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On 24 June 2016, I was informed by a colleague that [Baby O] had passed away."

blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: They have, yes.

blocks.text: In summary, what does this measurement report inform us of?

blocks.text: It shows that there's a mild metabolic acidosis.

The base excess and the bicarbonate levels were raised, suggesting there was a metabolic cause to the mild metabolic acidosis.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Could you explain the concept of a mild metabolic acidosis, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That would lean you more towards a problem that isn't ventilatory, like in a respiratory acidosis, the carbon dioxide level would be significantly raised. If the base excess and the bicarbonate are those levels, then the other category of causes would fall into things like infection or blood loss or fluid loss, that sort of thing, really.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So it's a pointer but not literally diagnostic of anything in particular?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Exactly, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I'm grateful. If we can go back to our tile 168 for a moment to see [Dr A]'s plan. So the plan was?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To do the gas, which we've just talked about, and he was suggesting that if there was any temperature instability, apnoea or bradycardia, so if [Baby O] were to stop breathing or his heart rate was to drop somewhat from the normal range or if there was any blood from anywhere, really, then that would be an indication for an abdominal X-ray to look at his tummy in more
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: detail and to consider giving fluid boluses, which would correct the metabolic acidosis.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. If we could look at some features of that plan in action. If we go to tile 180, I think we'll see a full blood count sample. Click on the original document, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So this is different to the last report that we looked at. How does it differ, Dr Brearey?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So this is a U&E result from the lab initially. It's showing a normal sodium level, a normal potassium level, the bicarbonate level is within normal range. Urea, normal. Creatine is slightly high by lab values but acceptable for a preterm neonate. And a bilirubin of 131, which I would have expected to be under the treatment line for jaundice.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So in summary, bilirubin apart, what do those results inform you of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: None of those results were concerning, in the normal range.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: All within normal range?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: When you say under the treatment line, that means it should have been --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No. There's a chart, which you may have seen, where you can plot the bilirubin level against time and there's a line, and if the level is above that then you give phototherapy or exchange transfusion if it's very high.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: But because it's below the line the baby didn't need treatment.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: That's what I thought because Mr Driver thought that that was concerning. So it wasn't in fact -- there wasn't any jaundice to speak of? Not requiring phototherapy?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It was mild, not needing treatment.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Before we get to your direct involvement, [Dr A] having suggested that --
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry, just can I --
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Because it just mentioned the CRP level being 1. So there was no evidence of infection on these blood tests either during this test and the full blood count result was similar. There was no concern about infection from the full blood count or the CRP.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Understood. Can I just ask you to consider X-rays, please. Firstly one at tile 197. If we look at Dr Wright's -- we don't need to go to the X-ray itself, Mr Murphy, if we just look at Dr Wrights' description or her radiology report, more accurately.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What did this reveal?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, I can go through her report if you like, but I think we agreed with this at the time, that the NG tube was in a satisfactory position with its tip in the stomach. There's a normal cardiac size and contour to the heart. Slightly increased lung density bilaterally, consistent with mild RDS. [Baby O] was on Optiflow at the time. Moderate gaseous distension of the bowel loops throughout the abdomen. No free peritoneal air, to indicate perforation, or intramural gas, to indicate necrotising enterocolitis. The appearance is non-specific, but NEC, necrotising enterocolitis, or mid-gut volvulus cannot be excluded.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: The doctor referred to a subsequent image which --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So I think [Baby O] had had a previous X-ray and the degree of distension of the bowel loops was improved from that previous X-ray.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I think if we go to our tile 246, and look at the summary of Dr Wright's consideration here, this is postintubation, so we have raced ahead in time a little.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This is 16.46, so this is after [Baby O] had had the bradycardia and desaturation and intubation. So it's an X-ray taken immediately after intubation to check the endotracheal tube position and it was reported that the endotracheal tube was in a satisfactory position, the NG tube should be advanced 10 to 15 millimetres, which seemed to be a little high in that X-ray. Normal cardiac size and contour. Mild bilateral changes of RDS, similar to the previous X-ray. The lungs appeared hyperinflated but there was no evidence of pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: The bowel was considerably less distended by comparison to the previous image earlier in the day.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: That was a reference that we saw, was it (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: On the previous one.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- Dr Wright's last report?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And no evidence of perforation or obstruction, and as you've already commented, no intramural or portal vein gas demonstrated?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Let's return to the chronology at tile 188. If we stay with the outer tile. It just records your arrival or entry within the unit. Does that accord with your recollection of your movements that day? So it's about 4.30ish you were passing there -- sorry, 2.30ish.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was earlier than that because I assisted with the intubation, which I think occurred around about 3, if I'm correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: It's my mistake. I said 4.30 and I should have said 2.30.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So you were on non-clinical duties, you told us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Teaching within the unit that day?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was a meeting. Either way it wasn't clinical, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And then if we go to the chronology at tile 199. Just to orientate themselves, go to the second tile there, which is [Dr A] recording that he, [Dr A], was called to see [Baby O] at 14.40 because of a desaturation, bradycardia and a mottled appearance.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Please tell us your recollection of when you became involved in these events.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: From my recollection, at some time between 14.40, when he had a desaturation, and about 15.00, 3 o'clock, when he was intubated. So at some time whilst [Dr A] was preparing and the
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: nursing staff were getting the medicines ready for the elective intubation.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And how did you come across the situation and what did you do in response?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was really supervising [Dr A]. He's a very senior registrar, so I didn't have any active role in the task.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: We went through the intubation checklist prior to intubation, which is checking the equipment and the personnel and allocating tasks for each role in the intubation. I was leading the intubation but [Dr A] was the first intubator allocated and if he was going to have trouble then I'd step in to be the second intubator. And then we went ahead and intubated [Baby O].
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we go to tile 206, please? Just click first on the original document and then we'll return to this page.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that your handwriting, Dr Brearey?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Are these notes written retrospectively and the notes were written at 18.00 or thereabouts on 23 June?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: They begin with the words:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "On the unit and assisted with intubation by [Dr A] this afternoon."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So you told us that you supervised or were on hand to supervise [Dr A]'s elective intubation of [Baby O] --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- which other information will tell us took place between 15.03 and 15.08 hours? So that's to fix it in time.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Tell us about the intubation process, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, [Dr A] didn't have any problems intubating and we worked together to fix the tube in the correct position and I clarified that there was a good colour change on the capnograph,
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: indicating that it was in the correct position and there was gas exchange going on.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And I listened to [Baby O]'s chest and there was good air entry on both sides. And it was -- we connected [Baby O] and the ET tube to the ventilator and started him on fairly normal ventilator settings for a preterm baby, really. The rate was 60 per minute. The inspiratory time on the ventilator was 0.4. The pressures were 20/6. And the amount of oxygen he's in initially was 30% oxygen, so not having to work too hard to ventilate [Baby O] at this stage, and he seems relatively stable.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So successively intubated to enable a connection to the ventilator?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: But in terms of the degree or extent of ventilatory assistance, was that moderate?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Moderate, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Next you have made a note of an observation you made.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you give us your recollection of that observation, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I noted during the intubation that [Baby O] had a rash on his chest, on the right side of his chest wall, exactly 1 or 2 centimetres in size. I haven't said the size there but I mentioned it in my statement. It was an unusual rash. It was initially -- it initially appeared like a purpuric rash.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Pausing there, Dr Brearey, you'll be more familiar with that term than most of us in the room. What do you mean by a purpuric rash?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I suppose most people might come across it when they're being warned what to look out for if children or babies have meningitis. So you talk about a glass test where you roll a glass over a rash and if it doesn't disappear, that means purpura because the little capillaries are broken under the skin and it is quite a worrying sign in a sick baby who presents to A&E, for example, with a temperature. So purpura in neonates is very, very rare and often babies are very ill when they have purpura.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So it was a little concerning and clearly noticeable. And I have made the point there of [Baby O] having good perfusion at the same time because you wouldn't expect a baby who is ill with sepsis, with purpura, to have good perfusion at the same time. It normally goes together that a baby has poor perfusion and a
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: poor capillary refill time and that didn't seem to be the case with [Baby O] at that time. So that's why I mentioned it in the notes. It was unusual.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: At that point in time did you form any view as to the possible cause for that presentation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, we've talked about sepsis already, and I was aware that [Dr A] had already started [Baby O] on antibiotics, so been restarted on IV cefotaxime already to cover for infection. I'm not entirely sure at this point whether we had the blood test back that we've just discussed with the CRP being 1, but certainly I think most doctors in that position would want to -- would have infection as their sort of first suspicion of a cause for this rash.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Did you have that as your first suspicion at that point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Initially, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You have told us that you were not a consultant on call, but you were on hand, so you lent your assistance.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you recall who was the on-call consultant for the neonatal unit that week?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: [Dr B].
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Did you communicate with [Dr B]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I did. I believe she was on the children's ward at the time when we intubated, so after I was happy that [Baby O] had stabilised after intubation, on my way back to my office, I stopped by to talk to [Dr B] to let her know that we had intubated [Baby O] and I think [Dr A] was about to do that as well anyway and give her an update around about the same time.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So [Baby O], having been connected to the ventilator, having intubated and then connected to the ventilator, more accurately, how was he, generally speaking, when you left and spoke to [Dr B]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: He seemed to have stabilised. We normally look to repeat a blood gas about half an hour after intubation to check that the numbers are all okay in terms of that.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So you don't have an immediate sort of definite idea, but there was nothing on the monitor or from the observations that were concerning at the point when he left at that time.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Before we move on through the chronology of events, you posed the question to yourself as to whether or not the blood results had been received at this point and I think, if we go to tile 175, which is earlier in time to that which we've just looked at -- this is actually the taking of a sample rather than the results.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we look at this document itself.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the blood culture was taken on that day looking for infection. There was no evidence of infection on blood culture as well as the CRP result being less than 1 that we've spoken about already.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: A culture taken at 13.39 that afternoon, but reported back in its fullness some 5 days later when no bacterial growth was discerned?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So let's move back to the chronology of events, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So you having assisted or supervised [Dr A], having left that part of the unit, spoken to [Dr B], were you then called back at 16.30 hours?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: If we could go to tile 205, please. What was happening — sorry, that doesn't appear to be the right tile. 225 perhaps. Go to tile 243, I'm told.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It wasn't 206 because that was the next one, written in retrospect at 18.00.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: 243, if we could click there, please. My note is in error.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Does this record, and if we go to your original, that you were called back to assist?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So I haven't included all of the background between that first paragraph and when I was called back to assist at 4.30, but from what I can gather from the notes, [Baby O] had a further deterioration on the ventilator, where he had a desaturation and a bradycardia on the ventilator that then prompted a re-intubation by [Dr A] and [Dr B], and then a further one secondary to that whilst on the ventilator. It was when they were assisting [Baby O] and managing [Baby O], the second of those re-deteriorations, that they called me to assist.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Both [Dr B] and [Dr A] will give evidence, out of sequence, but they'll be coming shortly.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's go to your note then at approximately 16.30.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What was happening when you came back to the NNU?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, [Baby O] had effectively been resuscitated by [Dr B] and [Dr A] and in that resuscitation effort he'd received two doses of adrenaline and had had cardiac compressions, and on my arrival he had restored to a spontaneous heart rate, increasing to 140, and oxygen saturations in the 90s when I arrived.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Sorry to interrupt, but could you give us an overview then of his state upon your arrival?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So on my arrival, he had restored his spontaneous circulation and his oxygen saturation levels were normal from a point, when [Dr B] and [Dr A] saw him, where he was having a bradycardia and desaturations.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. So you were informed, no doubt, of his condition when they intervened, but at the time you arrived --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- he was in some (overspeaking) recovery?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, they'd got him back again, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So what happened next?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I noted a good colour change on the capnograph and he became stable enough to be put back on to the ventilator, this time at slightly higher pressures. So the rate was the same, 60 per minute. His inspired oxygen concentration was 100% this time, which is higher than previously, and the pressures were 32/6, so higher peak pressures on the ventilator, so needing to do more work at that stage.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Could you expand upon that again as to why the ventilatory support was enhanced?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, it's hard to say other than the fact that those ventilator pressures were needed to maintain [Baby O]'s saturations and observations.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we go to tile 255, please. Could you explain to us the rationale behind the entries recorded here?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay. So on reassessing [Baby O] at that time, his perfusion wasn't as good as previously and we prescribed some dopamine, which is an infusion of medicine that raises the blood pressure. It's what we call an inotrope. So that infusion was started to help with his perfusion on the basis that his blood pressure might be a little low.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: FFP is fresh frozen plasma and that was requested.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Again, if you're considering sepsis then sepsis can cause something called disseminated intravascular coagulation coagulopathy, which essentially means there is clotting abnormalities as a result, so FFP would be the treatment for that. So that was requested. It needs to be taken out of storage and brought from the transfusion lab. So sometimes there's a little lead-in before it's actually given.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I think [Dr B] and [Dr A] had tried to do some capillary blood sample gases but weren't able to obtain those because of [Baby O]'s poor perfusion. But looking at his condition at the time, I felt that it would be reasonable to give him a half correction of sodium bicarbonate on the basis that he's more than likely still got that metabolic acidosis that I mentioned earlier.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Let's go to tile 263, please, as to the short infusion of sodium bicarbonate to enable us to understand.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What's the purpose, the objective, of the introduction of that at this point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, if a baby is acidotic then bicarbonate is essentially a base that corrects that acidosis. So that's the purpose of it, to increase the pH of the blood, and it's thought that the medication that we give, particularly things like dopamine, work better in a normal pH.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Tile 263, Mr Murphy. Sorry, that's where we are. Tile 267.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think it may be 266.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Sorry, 266.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: They all appear on these notes -- this is just a continuation, they're put into the sequence at this stage, but I'm retaining the one note and following it down on that note. I'm not criticising it, but you'll see it's just all on the one note and these various events go through. It's just further down this note, the same note.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Quite so.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: At 17.15 was [Baby O] baptised?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: How did he progress immediately thereafter?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: His heart rate started to drop towards the end of the baptism. So as the baptism finished then we intervened and started chest compressions and CPR.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: How significant a drop in heart rate is a drop down to the region of 60?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, less than 60 would be your criteria for starting chest compressions, less than 60 per minute.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. So chest compressions were started. Were you involved in the CPR?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Can you describe the process to us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, there is a standard neonatal life support process, so there will be three chest compressions to every one breath given through the ET tube at that time. That will continue with regular rechecks of the pulse and any effort at breathing that might have restarted. And then regular doses of adrenaline given during the resuscitation effort.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: As to the adrenaline, [Dr A] will give evidence as to the precise timing of that. But in terms of [Baby O]'s general appearance within the context of CPR, obviously, how did it appear to be going from a respiratory point of view?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, we had a really good team that afternoon, working really well, and so the process of the resuscitation, I couldn't fault it, to be honest, really. Everything was going as you'd expect. Dr Gibbs joined us at one stage, another senior member of staff. So there were three consultants present and a senior registrar who was going to be a consultant later that year. So we weren't short of experience.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Paediatricians are quite humble people, but Dr Gibbs and myself are both advanced paediatric life support instructors. I'm a neonatal life support instructor.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: [Dr A] and [Dr B] are very experienced. There was lots of years of experience in that resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: We were well supported by nursing staff and I thought clearly the process of the resuscitation and what we were doing was as I would have wanted or expected to happen. But we just weren't getting a response back in terms of [Baby O]'s condition that we'd normally expect from what I would consider to be a good quality resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Could I invite you to further analyse that response, please? We can see from the note that Neopuff inflations were underway and that there was good chest movement.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So we're quite confident that the Neopuff was being used but the endotracheal tube was still in situ and seeing his chest rise clearly is reassurance that the breaths that we're giving are inflating the chest and causing gas exchange in the lungs.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Was that gas exchange further evidenced by a capnograph reading?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So from that point of view, all was as one would hope in the circumstances?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: But did it have the desired effect?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It didn't seem to be having the effect we would normally see from those resuscitation efforts, no.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: What was the difference in [Baby O]'s presentation from that which one would anticipate you would "normally" see?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We'd normally see a response from heart rate initially, really, and the heart rate rising, and we didn't feel a pulse throughout this resuscitation. I've mentioned slightly lower down in the note that although the monitor was reading a heart rate between 40 and 200, he never had a palpable pulse. I believe I made a statement about this discrepancy to clarify this.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Could you explain that apparent discrepancy to us, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So there's different forms of cardiac arrest and the two main forms are cardiac arrest, where you don't have a pulse, either something we called asystole, where the monitor will have a flatline, or pulseless electrical activity, where the monitor might show some electrical activity in the form of a wave but
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: there's no palpable pulse. So effectively, the electricity is going through the heart but it is not enough for the heart to stimulate a heartbeat and generate that pulse pressure.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: From a practical point of view, it doesn't make a difference because you still need to carry on doing the CPR in the same way for both asystole and pulseless electrical activity.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And in [Baby O]'s case was there evidence on the monitor of electrical activity?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: However --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There was no pulse.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: What, if any, investigations did you undertake to try and solve the problem?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Obviously, with a sudden deterioration like this, we'd want to exclude a pneumothorax, so we did a cold light investigation and there was no suspicion of pneumothorax on cold light examination.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And of course we've already considered abdominal X-rays.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was there anything in any of those reports to suggest whether or not there was a pneumothorax?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: From the chest X-rays, no.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You've noted the consultants in attendance and the family members in attendance also.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: If we go to tile 286, we'll see the next page of your note. Could you explain to us what happened next as recorded in the note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay. So we'd been carrying on resuscitation for quite some time and it was starting to appear that there was no response to resuscitation and we'd been going for over half an hour since that baptism. I was aware that we hadn't had a blood gas for some time because previous attempts at blood gas had been unsuccessful because of the poor perfusion in [Baby O].
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I was also aware of previous deaths on the unit and the importance for us to show that we were resuscitating effectively. I could see it clinically in front of my eyes that
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: we were doing all those sorts of things properly, but sometimes having some blood tests help that and also a gas might help to help us in terms of our resuscitation as well, you know, if there were any specific abnormalities that we could correct. So I thought a blood gas would be helpful at this stage in proceedings.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: We didn't have a problem with IV access because the dopamine had been given, the adrenaline had been given, so we had IV access. But the problem with the peripheral IV access is that you can't take blood out of a peripheral cannula very easily, the vein collapses and you interrupt the infusions that are going through. And it was day 3 of life so the umbilical cord was quite dry and would have been quite difficult to cannulate, which would be the normal thing we do in a newborn baby.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: [Baby O] was 3 days old now and although [Dr A] had planned to put in a UVC prior to all these deteriorations, it can be a lengthy process and quite difficult to do at the best of times, even when someone is giving CPR. So I thought probably the best option at that time was an intraosseous blood sample.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Can you explain what that is, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the bones in -- a lot of long bones are hollow and within the hard bone itself is blood marrow and blood; that's where your blood cells are made. And, more so in paediatric practice for babies that come collapsed to the A&E department or older children to the A&E department, if the medical staff aren't able to get IV access soon, then the intraosseous route is the preferred option for getting quick access so you can do blood tests and give infusions.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So intraosseous needles have been used for some time for older babies and children, but not too commonly used in neonates. Their use is recommended now in neonatal life support courses but that change happened after these events, so it wasn't in any of the textbooks for neonatal life support at the time when these events were happening, but all of us, as paediatricians, knew how to take an intraosseous sample at least.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So the intraosseous needle wasn't needed to assist with the mechanics of the resuscitation because those fluids and the drugs had already been given. It was really, hopefully, a confirmatory blood test or a blood test to guide us in the late part of the resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. If anybody cares to note, the printout corresponds to -- Dr Brearey's handwritten note here is behind our tile 288, but we needn't go there, Mr Murphy, if we just stay with Dr Brearey's note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Looking at the next -- forgive me. Dealing with this in stages, so the results, the data there, from the blood test, what did that inform you of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The pH was just over 7, so [Baby O] still had an acidosis and it was still a metabolic acidosis. Importantly for me, as a doctor, as part of a team, the resuscitation team, the carbon dioxide level was 7.06, which told me that we were effectively ventilating [Baby O]'s lungs and that was the same carbon dioxide level as [Baby O] had in his previous gas early in the afternoon before any of these collapses. So whatever the cause of [Baby O]'s collapse, it didn't seem to be respiratory in origin from this.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: The base excess was raised, minus 17, which tells us about the metabolic cause for the acidosis. And the haemoglobin level was 86, which -- in retrospect, I was made aware of the initial post-mortem result, which suggested that there'd been a bleed from the liver into the abdominal cavity. And a haemoglobin level of 86 was less than the previous haemoglobin level from the lab tests, but it's still not a level that I would expect to be low enough to cause the collapses that occurred on that day.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: For a well baby, not on ventilatory support, we wouldn't give a blood transfusion for a haemoglobin of 86. So clearly, there'd been some blood loss and some dilution of the blood from all the fluids we'd been giving as well, but it's telling me now that I don't think blood loss on its own was the cause for the collapse or the collapses that [Baby O] had that day.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. I am looking now to the next three lines of your note, how was [Baby O]'s abdomen during the resuscitation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was still distended, and again we're at the point in the resuscitation where we're trying to exclude rarities that might have caused this. Rarely, I have only come across it once in a career, rather than a gas leak that causes a pneumothorax when a preterm baby is being ventilated, sometimes there can be a leak into the mediastinum, which is the central part of the chest where the heart sits. That can be called a pneumomediastinum. Again, on a rare number of occasions, that gas can leak down into the abdomen and cause the abdomen to be distended, which can then splint the diaphragm and stop the baby from breathing properly.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So in attempts to exclude that, I inserted a small cannula into the lower right corner of the abdomen in case that would decompress any free gas that had collected, but no gas came out of the cannula, just a small amount of blood, which was sent for culture, which more or less excluded that fairly rare event.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. We're now at 17.43, you having returned to [Baby O] at about 16.30 or thereabouts. We know that your previous involvement with him was at 14.40, at which point you told us that you noticed a rash on the right side of his chest wall during your first attendance upon him. Was there anything of note on his skin at this second occasion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That rash had disappeared, which tells me it definitely wasn't a purpuric rash because purpuric rashes don't vanish like that, they're around for a good few days afterwards, which is perplexing and I have never seen it before and I've not seen it since.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You told us earlier that purpuric rashes are the product of -- are infective in origin.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: What, if anything, is the relationship between that origin and the duration of the presentation of a purpuric rash?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't quite get your question.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Purpuric rashes, you have told us, are infective in origin.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Or can be, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Why is it that purpuric rashes don't disappear?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, there's rupture of the capillaries underneath the skin, so you know, it takes a while for that sort of thing to heal. It just doesn't vanish like that, really, in the space of an afternoon. You'd be seeing a purpuric rash for days and weeks afterwards usually before it fades completely and the skin heals.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. So you had inserted a cannula in, it's technically referred to as the McBurney's point to exclude or, if present, address this rare condition that you explained to us, but you were able to rule that out effectively. Then, please, could you describe to us the remainder of the attempted resuscitation process?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The parents were present for at least some of the resuscitation, but not all of it. I can actually remember seeing more of the grandmother than I can of the parents, just from memory, but they were updated by myself and the team throughout the resuscitation. And obviously, a very distressing time for everybody, really, the family and the team involved. But it
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: became increasingly present at that time that we had worked really hard and just simply, and unusually, weren't getting a response to those resuscitation efforts and the team agreed that to continue resuscitation was going to be futile. That again was discussed with the parents and grandmother, and then we withdrew care and stopped our resuscitation efforts and passed [Baby O] to his mum.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Your note suggests that occurred after a full 30 minutes of attempted resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At least, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: At least?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: We know that in time, [Baby O]'s case was referred to the coroner. Did you involve yourself with that process at all?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No. [Dr B] was the consultant of the week, so she spoke to the coroner afterwards.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: But did you hold a debrief for the neonatal staff involved?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I did, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: What, if any, conclusions did you draw from this set of events?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was... All these events in the trial, you know, are distressing for staff, but both [Baby O] and [Baby P]'s deaths were particularly distressing for those involved and equally so with me, really. But there was clearly some elements of the case that I was concerned about. All three triplets were born in such good condition and were following a path, healthy path, to growing and developing and hopefully going home, and you know, the deterioration of [Baby O] that day really came out of the blue as far as that was concerned and the fact that we had to intervene initially felt like a surprise and the fact that each time we tried to stabilise him and resuscitate him we got to a period of stabilisation and then he deteriorated soon afterwards. The fact that he had two desaturations and bradycardias on the ventilator is exceptionally unusual when we're so confident that things were fine with him.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: The rash was unusual and like nothing I'd seen before or since, and we'd excluded as many, if not all, natural causes for him collapsing like this and I couldn't then, and I can't now, think of a natural cause for why these events happened.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Did those concerns prompt you to take a particular course in relation to reporting the events within the hospital system?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. I intended to escalate it the following day, but [Baby P] had already started deteriorating and I was helping with some of his care the following day already. We'd had -- so following [Baby P]'s passing, I attended the debrief for [Baby P]'s care the following day and I've worked quite closely with Dr Rackham, who was actually leading that debrief. He was the transport consultant who was present at the time.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: From Arrowe Park?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: From Arrowe Park, yes. Nurse Letby was present in that debrief. I asked her how she was feeling and I can remember suggesting to her that she would need the weekend off to recover from these traumatic events. She didn't seem overly upset to me in the debrief, or upset at all, and told me at the time that she was on shift the next day, which was a Saturday. I was concerned about this because we'd already expressed our concerns to senior management about the association with Nurse Letby and the deaths we'd seen on the unit.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So following the debrief, I phoned the duty exec on call in the hospital that evening, Karen Rees, she is the senior nurse in the urgent care division, who was on call. She was familiar with our concerns already and I explained what had happened and that I didn't want Nurse Letby to come back to work the following day or until this was all investigated properly.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Karen Rees said no to that and that there was no evidence. The crux of the conversation then went that I put it to her that was she happy to take responsibility for this decision in view of the fact that myself and my consultant colleagues all wouldn't be happy with Nurse Letby going to work the following day, and she responded, yes, she would be happy to take that responsibility.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I said, well, would you be happy with the responsibility if anything were to happen to any of the babies tomorrow then, and she said, yes, she would be able to take that responsibility. That's where the conversation finished.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: For the sake of completeness -- sorry, I interrupted.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We had further conversations with the execs the following week when action was taken.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Sorry for interrupting. Tile 498 is a Datix form submitted by Nurse Letby but within which you're mentioned. If we go to the original form, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Are you familiar with the format of this document?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: In a sentence, what is its purpose?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So we have a Datix incident reporting system in the hospital, so this can be entered by any member of staff, clinical or non-clinical, if they feel an incident has happened, however small or large, and we had a very healthy culture in terms of incident reporting in the neonatal unit at the time. One of my jobs as neonatal lead doctor was to review these incidents and act on them appropriately in terms of learning for staff and to try and treat it as a sort of no-blame culture, if you like.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So the format -- do you want me to go through it?
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: The name of the patient is [Baby O]. The location was on the neonatal unit in the urgent care division.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: If we can scroll down.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: First of all, the date. Go up to the date. The reported date is 30 June. The opened date is 1 July.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Okay. So that would have been reported then a week after.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Yes. If you could direct Mr Murphy to scroll down.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So the risk grading is a near miss. "Actual harm" is none. "Potential for harm" is high potential harm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I think that the first two of those are recorded by the person reporting it and then the potential for harm is an automatic thing that comes out on the system.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I haven't seen this. I can't recall reviewing this Datix. I might have done.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: If we go to incident investigation, there's a reference to your name, Dr Brearey.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Annemarie Lawrence was the risk facilitator for us at the time.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: It says, "Reviewed in the NNIRG meeting", that's the Neonatal Incident Review Group, by myself, Eirian Powell, who's the neonatal unit manager, Annemarie Lawrence I have mentioned, Ailsa Simpson was a senior nurse, and Gemma Webster was a pharmacist. It says:
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: "SB [that's me] wishes amendment to incident form. Patient did not lose peripheral access. Intraosseous access required for blood samples only."
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Is that just you correcting part of a narrative?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I haven't seen the actual report.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: If you go back up, I think you'll see reference to that further up.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Description." It says:
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: "Infant had a sudden acute collapse requiring resuscitation. Peripheral access lost. Intraosseous access required. Resources not available on unit.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: "Action taken: staff obtained equipment from children's ward. Delay in this happening due to staff being needed for infant care needs. LP needle utilised as time delay in obtaining."
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So what I didn't mention in terms of getting an intraosseous sample is that the most common way of doing that in older children and term babies is something called an EZ-IO device. Prior to that, it was literally a big needle with a bit of a screw -- and this sounds brutal, sorry, but you screw it into the shinbone of the baby. Obviously it's a resuscitation situation. If you haven't done it before, that can be quite daunting for staff, whereas an EZ-IO needle is easier to do. It just resembles a mini hand drill with a magnet on the end of it where the needle sits on the end of it.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So you literally just -- you just put it up against the baby's skin, where it ought to go against the bone, and just press the button and it drills through to the core of the -- middle of the bone for you. So the neonatal unit didn't have an EZ-IO device on the neonatal unit -- and I don't think many neonatal units in the country at that time would have had EZ-IO devices to use, although most paediatric A&E departments probably would have done, which is why the doctors were familiar with them.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So from my recollection, when I said let's do an IO, I think somebody might have gone to look for the EZ-IO device, which would have been on the children's ward, and from my recollection I said, don't worry, we can just use a needle, which was
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: adapted, a short LP needle, which I've used before in previous haematology jobs in babies, this sort of size (indicating), and I put the needle in because I think it would have been quicker than waiting for the EZ-IO device, really.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So there was no delay and there was no problem with IV access, it was only for a blood sample. So it wasn't really an incident, to be honest, because we just got on and did it anyway.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So is it accurate or inaccurate to assert that peripheral access was lost?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's inaccurate, untrue.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And so was there at all relevant times intravenous access to [Baby O]'s circulation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At least one and sometimes two, at times two. I think it's recorded in the notes somewhere that a second IV access was obtained in the record.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Could you remain there, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: You're going to be more than a few minutes, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: More than that, my Lord, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (A short break)
Mr Driver, I notice the family are not here.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you for that.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

Can I just check, is everybody here who wants to be here? Thank you very much.
