Obviously, in retrospect, after seeing the post-mortem results and seeing that there was a ruptured subcapsular haematoma, that's probably the most likely place where the blood came from, is that ruptured subcapsular haematoma of the liver.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I am just going to pause there so we can keep track of this. We have heard already in this case with regard to [Baby O] that one of the findings after he died was that there had been a haematoma, there'd been a bleed of some sort to the liver and we'll hear more about that. We have mentioned that before so I am just making sure we can all keeping track of what you're referring to by the subcapsular haematoma. That's whatever it was that was the bleed to the liver?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: When you refer to it's not -- it may not have been the words you used, so forgive me, but not a surprising or it's something you might expect to find after this stage of the resuscitation, when talking about the blood are you referring to the fact that because of resuscitation it's possible that there may be some bleeding internally because of the efforts being made?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Potentially, yes, or the lack of oxygen to the tissues (overspeaking). It's impossible to say with any certainty.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: It's possible -- sorry?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Looking at -- McBurney's point is -- if you draw a line between the umbilicus, the tummy button, and the bony prominence, the iliac crest of the pelvis, the McBurney point is two thirds way along that, so it is quite low down on the righthand side of the tummy. Even looking at the final X-ray, which did appear to show a slightly enlarged liver, putting a needle in that point in the abdomen was nowhere near where the liver was.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So your opinion is if it's picked up the blood or the blood it picked up might have tracked there from somewhere else but not that the needle has gone into an organ?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It wouldn't have gone into the liver.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: All right. But your view is that haematoma, we are talking about the subcapsular haematoma, that might have ruptured during resuscitation efforts?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It might have done.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I want to turn then to other matters. That's what I wanted to ask you in fact about the clinical side of this. But there's other things you told us about, Dr Brearey, that I want to ask you about, just for a little bit more information.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We know, and you have referred to it, that by this time on the unit, so far as you and some of the consultants were concerned, there's a link between the presence of Ms Letby and events that took place.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All the consultants.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: All the consultants knew at this point, did they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Right. And that's based on the fact, as it seemed to you or them, that she'd been on the unit at the time of potentially significant events? That was the unifying feature, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was one of them, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: That was one of them? All right. We'll see what others there are.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: When Dr Jayaram gave evidence back in -- the last time, which was 28 February, he referred to the fact that he'd been careful, in effect, to avoid confirmation bias. That's an expression you're aware of, isn't it, confirmation bias?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Confirmation bias, and I'll ask if you agree with this, give a different explanation if you want to, is the tendency to focus on information that tends to support an existing opinion or belief, the tendency to focus on that rather than other factors. As a definition, do you agree with that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it's a tendency to try and confirm your beliefs —
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- with preconceived ideas.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And you tend to fix upon those things which meet those beliefs and maybe not things which would steer away from them?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Being aware of confirmation bias is very useful because then you can try and avoid it as best you can.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You can try to.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We try to be as objective as possible.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I'm afraid you'll have to speak up, Dr Brearey. We were just getting to grips with confirmation bias and I'd suggested a very basic definition and you were just explaining or agreeing, to this extent, it's the tendency to see things which back up what you might already think?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is bias, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You said that you are aware of that so you try to avoid it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Although, of course, sometimes someone may not even know when they're doing it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Some may not.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Now, after the death of [Baby D], which was back at the end of June 2015, it's after that, isn't it, that you first performed a review of any common features and first identified that Ms Letby had been on duty on the incidents you were looking at?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I didn't identify it. Eirian Powell identified it when she did a staffing analysis after the first three deaths in June 2015.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Is that something you'd asked her to do?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Was it something you were actively interested in knowing whether there was any unifying factor?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was the purpose of the meeting.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Yes. So Eirian Powell, who we have met once, relatively briefly, in this case, she in effect was the nursing manager for the unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She was. So we had a meeting, I can't remember whether it was late June or early July 2015, with the director of nursing, then Alison Kelly, and the head of risk, and three deaths in a short period of time were a concern, but at the same time statistically if we had no more deaths that year, it would still be within the normal range for our unit's mortality rates.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And Eirian Powell looked at all the possible things that might be common to these deaths that can be looked at, which was more than just a staffing analysis. She did the staffing analysis and associated that link, but she also looked at which incubator spaces the babies were in, whether they had been on certain pumps, you know, any factor.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: We looked at microbiology, any factor that might be a common link between all of them and there didn't seem to be anything like that. It was my job prior to the meeting to sort of correlate the clinical care reviews and look at whether there were any links in terms of that that might explain the deaths.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: All right. It's from that point, the end of June 2015, that certainly you have or had identified to you the presence of Ms Letby on three of those events?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct. I think my comment in the meeting at the time was, "No, it can't be Lucy, not nice Lucy".
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: We'll come to your views on that in a little bit.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it wasn't my view, it was my view at the time.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: All right. Dr Jayaram also was party to that, wasn't he, to that knowledge at that time?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Dr Jayaram wasn't at the meeting, but obviously he was the clinical lead at the time.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Yes. So you'd have shared that with him soon afterwards?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I shared it with all my colleagues because it was a meeting about the deaths in the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So everybody knew that, to that extent at least, Ms Letby was an object of interest from June -- by everyone I mean your consultant colleagues knew by June 2015 that Ms Letby was a subject of interest?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I certainly emailed Dr Jayaram. I can't remember emailing my other colleagues, although we might have discussed it, I can't remember.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You remember emailing Dr Jayaram?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: When I asked you, "Did you share that with Dr Jayaram", your immediate response was to say you shared it with all your colleagues.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I didn't say when. I can't remember when I shared it with all of them, but over the course of the rest of the year, I would have shared it with them at some stage.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I'm not disputing that is a focus of concern for you, Dr Brearey.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, the deaths and the collapses were a focus of my concern.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I do suggest that once Ms Letby had been identified as somebody or a factor that was common to those, there was naturally a bias against her in terms of how she behaved was interpreted; do you agree or disagree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I disagree.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Right. We know, and you touched on this in your evidence, there's no formal complaint made to the police at any point right up to the period we're dealing with, with [Baby O], is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, identifying the cause for death is quite important in identifying concerns. And the process of identifying the cause of death is a long process. You know, the coroner's inquest that occurred for some of these babies that died in June didn't complete until later on in 2016. There's learning from every case that we reviewed and that's normal. You know, there's no one episode of care in the NHS where everything's completely perfect and we would pick up learning points from each episode, but they were just learning points, they didn't explain why these babies collapsed always.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: But that was my job. My job wasn't to identify the cause of death, that was the sort of coronial process, if you like, for inquests and the like. But my job was to try and improve our practices and over the course of that year our practices did improve and get better.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: They were already good before this all started and our results in a number of factors would back that statement up. But as the year went on and more events happened, then more suspicion arose, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Yes, I'm looking at the question of suspicion. If someone close to you was attacked or hurt unlawfully by somebody, Dr Brearey, and you believed you knew the identity of that person, you'd contact the police and give it to them, wouldn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If I saw an act happening, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And if you believed you knew the identity of the perpetrator?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If I saw that act happening, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Yes. And if -- maybe not as dramatic as that. If someone were to burgle your house, heaven forbid, but if they did and you believed you knew the identity of the perpetrator, you would be ready to report that to the police?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Or of they stole your car?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And if someone hurt one of the babies on your unit and you believed you had the identity of the person responsible, you'd report that to the police too, wouldn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think you're making this a little bit more simplistic than it actually was because it's not something that anybody wants to consider, considering that a member of your staff is harming babies. And actually, the senior nursing staff on the unit didn't believe this could be true up until the point when the -- you know, and beyond, when [Babies O & P] died.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: But the year was spent for predominantly myself and Dr Jayaram, but also my colleagues, with increasing suspicion with every episode, and none of us wanted to believe it either. But the fact that things in terms of practices were going from good to better, the fact that we were working on a very good unit that normally had very good results, and this all became very exceptional, and then when we stopped to take a step back and think about it, the nature of these collapses, as you've heard this morning already, the unexpected nature of them, the lack of response to resuscitation, the unusual rash that had been noted on a number of occasions, and each time the association with Nurse Letby -- and that is nothing to do with confirmation bias, that's just statistically every time it happened it became statistically more and more improbable and that was raising our concerns to a point where, yes, that was... That's when we escalated when we did.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I'm not disputing with you the question of suspicion at all --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The other thing to say as well is that nobody was flagging a concern to us from outside the hospital. The coroners, the pathologists, the neonatal network, MBRRACE
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: reports come back a year or two after the actual -- that's the national mortality reporting for women and babies. That comes back 2 years later, which is all very unusual in some ways for the NHS, where you tend to get a lot of pressure to do things and act on things, and yet we were getting this mortality this year, and there wasn't any red flags being alerted outside the trust or within it.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So I was very keen to take another opinion, get somebody without any confirmation bias, and that's why we had a review of the deaths that had occurred up and through 2015 and that review took place in February 2016 eventually, with an external neonatologist from Liverpool Women's Hospital, to review all our reviews and to review the cases and provide some sort of external sense to things for these cases.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Twelve months, approximately, is the period of, certainly for you and Dr Jayaram, suspicion, about Ms Letby, isn't it, from [Baby D] to [Baby O]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well --
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: It is, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, 12 months of knowledge of her association with these cases.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Increasing knowledge or suspicion then? Put it that way.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, knowledge of an increasing association, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And the reason I'm going to suggest nothing was actually done about it, so far as she is concerned, is because you appreciate that, apart from her being present on the unit or apparently present at the time of potentially relevant events, that was as far as that went. That's as far as it got so far as she is concerned?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Certainly that was a major factor but I have just talked to you about the increasing evidence of worry and that was really put down on paper during that review in February 2016, where it was noted that the majority of cases where the babies collapsed occurred at night, where less staff and parents were present, in the early hours, that a lot of the deteriorations were sudden collapses.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: That's an example I am going to suggest of confirmation bias in the sense that you're identifying factors that linked in some way to Ms Letby. That's what you were naturally doing, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Ms Letby wasn't mentioned in that meeting until the end of the meeting and all those observations were made by Dr Subhedar, a senior neonatologist from Liverpool Women's Hospital, who made those observations before I even brought up the fact that there was an association with Nurse Letby.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Your interpretation of that and the factors you're picking out and the way you say that feeds into your suspicion is part of the confirmation bias in having decided it's to do with her in the first place.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Dr Subhedar didn't have any confirmation bias because he didn't know the association at that time and he still came up with those factors that we included in the reports that were common to all the cases.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: But he's not drawing a link to Nurse Letby in the way you are, Dr Brearey.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, because we're in court now, aren't we, and a lot more has come to light since then.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And from what you were saying, did you contact the police in February 2016 when you did that review if it took you to the place you tell us it took you to?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It didn't take me to that place immediately and it also didn't exhaust the avenues within the trust of escalating my concerns. So following that thematic review, I completed the report and sent it to the director of nursing and also the head of safety and quality, who's the director of nursing, and the medical director of the hospital, asking for an urgent meeting with them along with Eirian Powell, the neonatal unit manager. That was my escalation following that meeting.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: One thing, for instance, you didn't look at closely, I'm going to suggest to you, is the question of the acuity of the babies who were being brought under the unit and a significant increase in the numbers of high acuity babies over the period. That wasn't the sort of thing you were focusing on, was it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, in my opinion, and was backed up from the BadgerNet data that we all use in the country for neonatal care, there wasn't a significant increase in acuity and, anyway, you could argue it's either a chicken or egg. You know, I'm sure you'd want to argue that an increase in acuity caused all these cases, which personally I find completely unfeasible. Or you could argue that the cases themselves created an increasing acuity in the unit because of the more intensive care we were providing in the unit because of the sudden collapses, which I think is much more likely.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Do you agree that increases in acuity could be a relevant factor?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't think it was a relevant factor in these cases.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Well, I'm going to suggest to you that's one example of the type of bias that I'm suggesting took place taking place.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I would be quite happy to take that criticism from an expert witness who is experienced in neonatology.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Right. So you are not able to tell us then whether you considered high acuity as relevant?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It was considered as part of it, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And quite simply, it's not something you regarded as significant?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If you look at all the cases I don't think there was a single case in any of the ones we reviewed at that review in February where there was a lack of staff that had any significant effect on the cases.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So you disregard any question about staff numbers playing any part to do with any element of care?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In any of these cases there was not a single episode that we reviewed where a lack of staff contributed to the outcome of the babies.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So not high acuity, not any problems with staff. What about any sub-optimal performance by any other member of staff on your unit? Is that something you identified and actioned?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Would you like to define how you (overspeaking) suboptimal --
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I'm just asking you, did you do that. Anything below understand outside the guidelines and not done in the right way?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If you're saying optimal means perfect I'd say things aren't always perfect. But I don't think our practices and our care that we were receiving (sic) was any different than it would have been in any other local neonatal unit in the region, and probably the country.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: In fact, in some ways it was a lot better.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I'm going to suggest to you didn't go about looking for sub-optimal performance in any way with regard to anyone else. You were interested in establishing the link between Ms Letby and the events we are looking at in this case.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I would completely disagree with that because in every case we identified elements of care that could be improved on. What I'm saying is those elements of care would not have affected the very tragic results that occurred with these babies.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: That's your view on that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: My view on it is that we identified areas that could be improved on, but none of them had an effect on the final outcome.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I'm going to suggest to you that the possibility of it being down to one person in the way you were suspecting is something that is attractive in the context of confirmation bias rather than looking for problems like acuity --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely not.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- or sub-optimal performance.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely not. I'd much rather not have to sit here today and talk to you and have something that we could get our teeth into and improve in terms of patient care.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: But as I say I was very happy that the care and the team that was working were excellent.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I make it plain, Dr Brearey, that I'm not challenging that you had the suspicion that you've described, that's not what I'm challenging. But what I do want to suggest to you is that the reason that the police were not contacted at any point during the period with these babies in the unit that we have been looking at is because you appreciated that, beyond Ms Letby's presence on certain occasions, there was nothing to get beyond that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The reason we didn't go to the police was because we wanted to escalate this appropriately within the structure of the hospital rather than directly going to the police ourselves without the support of the medical director and the executives in the trust.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You'd go to the police if your car was stolen and you knew who did it, wouldn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As I say, I don't think that's the correct analogy.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And if you believe that somebody's harming babies on your unit on your watch, if you believed that for sure, then you would be able and you would have acted on that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I try to act on facts rather than belief --
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- and that's what I was doing.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Yes. I am not going to challenge that. It's a question of belief, not facts?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I was acting on facts.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Not belief?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Not belief.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Well --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's what he said.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. You have suspicion, but the reason you didn't contact the police is that there was no basis for that to say someone had done something wrong?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Of course there was a basis, but we were trying to escalate appropriately to our executives at the time with the facts that we had at the time.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Nothing would stop you, or any of your colleagues, raising it, in effect blowing the whistle, at the point you wanted to within the NHS if there was a good reason for doing that, would it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, there was a very good reason to escalate to our executives because of the facts of the case that I have just talked about: the association with Nurse Letby, the nature of the collapses, the fact that they're happening suddenly overnight and the lack of response to resuscitation and the rashes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You make it sound as if the executive you have referred to, Karen Rees, wasn't really that concerned by your concerns.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, because she believed that Nurse Letby couldn't have done this.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And you believed otherwise?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I didn't believe, I was worried about the facts of the case -- all the cases.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And if you were anxious about the babies on your unit with the solid facts that you say you had, then the next obvious thing to do would be to escalate it, for example, to the police, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. It would be to talk to the executives, to try and confirm the correct plan of action going forward. I've not gone to the police before with concerns about multiple deaths on a neonatal unit and I'm not sure many neonatal leads have done. It needed executive support and that's what we were after.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You don't even -- we went to a Datix form. That Datix form is about intraosseous needles, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You ended up saying it's not really an incident at all, was your evidence on that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, no.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: It just doesn't raise any issue regarding Lucy Letby, does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: There's not even a Datix form submitted about her, about your suspicions.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Are you expecting me to Datix the fact that I'm worried that a nurse might be harming babies on the unit?
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Somebody might expect, if you had 12 months thinking that, you might do something, Dr Brearey.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I was doing as much as I could do at the time.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Dr Rackham, was he a consultant who came to deal with the transport and assist late in the resuscitation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, he's a neonatologist.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I am looking at the question of confirmation bias still, so we keep focus on this. In fact, in the review that took place, he commended Lucy Letby for her work during the resuscitation, didn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I've got the statement that you made to the police here about this in November 2017. I just want you to have a look at page 39 where you make reference to this.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's going to be shown to and you his Lordship and the barristers, the lawyers.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just have a look to yourself, please, where we have:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Following these deaths Dr Rackham led a debrief. "
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If you just read that and the lines that follow it.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: (Pause)
Have you read that to yourself?
Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You mentioned about how Nurse Letby was. What you were dealing with here was you told the police in 2017 that Dr Rackham had led the debrief and he commended Nurse Letby. You then said to the police this:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I had a conversation with Nurse Letby suggesting she should have the weekend off and not return to work but she refused. I expressed my concerns to Karen Rees who was the duty manager that day but without success. Karen Rees gave me the impression..."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, she didn't agree with you and she didn't think it was a reasonable request to make.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: "Completely subjectively, on the morning [Baby O] died I was just passing through the unit and I walked past Nurse Letby she was upbeat, happy and more confident than normal. She said, 'Hello, Dr Brearey', and looked me in the eye very confidently."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's something you saw fit to put in your statement to the police, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it was just what happened.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Yes, but that's an example of you, for instance, interpreting her walking past, being as you describe, you say
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: upbeat, happy and more confident, and picking that out as something worthy of comment in a police statement; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And, no doubt, I'm going to suggest, if she'd walked past you and looked the other way with a stony face, that would find its way in as well? If she'd looked away from you that would appear there, wouldn't it, interpretation of things in a negative light because of confirmation bias, Dr Brearey?
