And if that doesn't happen over a period of time, your heart, because it's not getting oxygen either, starts to drop, which again is a very bad sign.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Notwithstanding that, you've got -- is that:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Good air entry on auscultation"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So I would have straightaway gone in -- because this baby was intubated, so when they are being bagged you can listen in and I could hear that the air was moving on auscultation. But his oxygen saturations weren't coming up. So if you're delivering breaths and you're delivering oxygen and you're bagging through a patent tube, you would expect that baby's oxygen levels and heart rate to respond and come up.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: What I have said is:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Good air entry on auscultation. Saturations not improving."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you want me to carry on?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'll assist you, if I may. You have then noted that the ETT was removed and [Baby O] was re-intubated --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- by [Dr A] with a size 3 at first attempt.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you recall, it doesn't seem to be in your note, what [Baby O]'s reaction to that was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I don't exactly recall, but what I would say is that if [Baby O] had resisted or we had had to do a forced -- because when babies are active, they resist by breathing or breathing
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: against or showing some movement, which can make intubation a bit challenging. Babies who, what we call, are completely flat, you know, their oxygenation and heart rate will just lie there and you can do anything to them. So that, from my note and from my memory -- there was no time literally to say, "Well, let's get some drugs", and basically he was flat as it is.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the intubation, first attempt -- again, [Dr A] is a very experienced registrar, he's very good at what he does. Secondly, it doesn't seem like there was a situation where we had problems intubating him.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. But despite that, by 16.15, you are recording again bradycardia with desaturation. So this is after the second tube --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- has been placed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So does that rule out any problem with the ventilator itself or certainly the tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So this is re-intubation and this probably is -- the second intubation or re-intubation would have been done just in case: yes, I can hear the air entry okay, but because his saturations aren't coming up, I'm going to give this the benefit of doubt and re-intubate just in case. Because there's no 100% guarantee, if I can hear good air entry, there can't be a problem with the tube.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So in between that time, with first attempt, what I have not written, but I'm assuming his saturations would have come up and his heart rate would have come up as well and then he drops again with heart rate dropping again to 60 and saturations dropping to 50%.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. 50%, what would you say about that level? You told us about 35 --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Very poor. Very poor.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He was hand ventilated using the Neopuff; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So we would take these babies off the ventilator and then you would manually give breaths while watching the baby and seeing if their chest is moving, and obviously looking at the
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: monitor if the heart rate and the saturations are coming up, that manoeuvre.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Do you recall who was hand ventilating on that occasion? No?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Now, the heart rate you have recorded at 60 and we've heard from other witnesses, correct me if I'm wrong, that's the point at which it's dangerously low and chest compressions become necessary?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And you have put on the next line that that in fact is what commenced at 4.30 pm or 16.30 on your note?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We've also heard that there's a set protocol for the purposes of resuscitation. Is that, given the situation which had now arisen, what kicked in at that point at 4.30?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Hence your note about adrenaline. Is that bicarbonate being administered?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You've put there that [Dr A]'s entry, or you've inferred there, correct me if I'm wrong, is more detailed in this regard; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So basically, going back, I have made the retrospective note at 6 o'clock. The resuscitation drugs are given at certain times and somebody's responsible for recording the first adrenaline given at this time, second, third, however many. And at that point, that record -- so we were probably all documenting similar things because there were quite a few people who had been involved. So I didn't translate all that in my documentation, saying that [Dr A]'s entry notes... and in the resus chart which would have the exact timings and dose of those drugs that were given.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We're expecting [Dr A] tomorrow, so I'm not going to take you to that note, but others may.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Your next entry deals with a left great saphenous cannulation; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just tell us about that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So basically, earlier in the day, when [Dr A] had reviewed [Baby O] about the abdominal distension and a blood gas that had been done, which was not very good, he had cannulated [Baby O] and started him on intravenous fluids and organised an abdominal X-ray. So [Baby O] had one intravenous access.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: When children or babies become unwell, we are mindful of trying to get more than one intravenous access for various reasons. One is if you lose that one then you've got nothing. Secondly, we have to give multiple drugs, not all of them are compatible with each other and sometimes you think, well, okay, if I can use this one for this and that one for that -- so I think we were all very conscious that we had just one intravenous access for [Baby O]. So quite a few people were trying -- I think I've put, maybe not here, but in my statement, [Dr A] tried a few times, so he would have been at one end, and normally just one person would try at a time and once I'd seen him have a couple of attempts -- I think I've put three attempts -- I started at the -- because I was at his foot end. So I tried the -- the saphenous vein is a big vein in your lower leg, just by the ankle.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: And one of the things with big veins is you can -- it looks like I didn't get a lot of flashback, there was a little bit of blood probably because his circulation was so poor. When I flushed it, the cannula flushed, so that IV access was secured.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was about to ask you about that next entry. So were you satisfied that that was a functional intravenous access?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So I've said, "Not bleeding back much". That means that -so when you cannulate -- the saphenous vein is a big vein, so normally in a child who has good circulation, blood literally flows back and drips and we have to be sort of -- you have to press on the top to stop the blood from coming, but this did not happen. So there would have been a flashback and I could see that a little bit of blood was coming through, but I didn't feel that at that time the priority was collecting blood.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And sometimes if you move things around too much you can actually lose the access and I was conscious that this was a precious access and I needed to save it for administering medication rather than getting blood.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And you can check -- if you're not in the vein, you get a big swelling at the end, so I would have flushed it and checked that it's going where it needs to go.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And if I wasn't in the vein, it would have been obvious that I was not in the vein and there was a swelling proximal to where I had cannulated and the cannula would have been taken out.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. So you satisfied yourself that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. There would have been other people around me, it's not just one person, because when you flush, other people are looking as well just to confirm that we are happy with this.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was going to ask you, after the word "flushed", is that "fine" in brackets?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So I have confirmed that it flushed and it flushed fine.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then you indicate -- is that "dopamine commenced"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we scroll down a bit further please, Mr Murphy:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Three attempts at capillary gas unsuccessful."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just explain that to us, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. In the first instance, if we had managed to get some blood from the cannulation, that would have been checked for a venous gas. This again -- capillary gases are -- with babies we -- there are little lancets that you pierce their heel with and then you squeeze, and little drops of blood come out that you collect in a little capillary. It looks like his perfusion was so poor that there was no blood from --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So not even the prick with the pin was producing any blood?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Dr A] [is that], Dr Brearey and myself present at resuscitation from 4.30 pm onwards"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When Dr Brearey arrived, I went and discussed with..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that Dr Rackham?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From transport?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So just explain to us then, was that, for the time being, your involvement in what was going on?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So basically, at this time -- so when I've said about 4.30, this is the time when we'd given the adrenaline, the bicarb, we had an IV access, we'd started the dopamine and at that time he was put back on the ventilator. I had asked for Dr Brearey to come -- I think this is mentioned later on, I can hold on and come back to it later. But my main purpose of asking for him -- the things going through my mind was what had caused his sudden collapse, what had happened. One of the things I was thinking was: can it be something to do with his heart?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dr Brearey has a specialist interest in cardiology and we often ask for his help when we suspect underlying cardiac problems, to do echocardiograms. That's why I'd asked for Dr Brearey to come down and assess whether -- and I haven't documented --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Let's deal with that now.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did that happen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That did happen. So Dr Brearey came down. We had a discussion, and again I have not documented that in great detail here, but I have done in my statement.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dr Brearey -- obviously, I think you probably already know that Dr Brearey had been present earlier on when [Dr A] had intubated, so he had supervised that intubation. I didn't know that at the time when Dr Brearey came down and I was explaining to him what had happened. He assessed the baby and his opinion was that this wasn't a cardiac cause for this collapse and he didn't feel that an echocardiogram was required.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We've heard a little bit about the process of differential diagnosis. Is this working through the possibilities if it's simply -- to eliminate them?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Absolutely, yes. And because Dr Brearey was there as an overseeing consultant and the registrar was there, we had a discussion about thinking about different differential diagnoses
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: and one of the outcomes of the discussion was: let's discuss with a tertiary centre neonatologist, give them an update on what's happened, ask if they have anything else to advise that we haven't thought of or done, and also given that [Baby O] has become so poorly, would he be transferred to a tertiary neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So twofold, really. Advice, if they can offer anything different, and also the possibility of a transfer if it became necessary?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you remember going away to speak to Dr Rackham?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you remember where you'd have gone to do that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: As far as I can remember, I went to -- I think it's called the resource room. So as you enter the doors there's a room to the right and that was probably the -- usually the nurses would go there for their breaks, the doctors would as well. It was relatively further out and you can close the door. So there's other parents, patients, everywhere else, including at the reception of the nursing station. So I didn't want to have that conversation in the middle of the unit, so I think that's where I went.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That would have afforded some privacy?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. Following your conversation with Dr Rackham did you go back into the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Oh yes, yes. I never left the unit. So this is within the unit.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Overspeaking).
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, to nursery 1, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And what was the situation when you went back the second time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I'll have to go back on to...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Pause there, doctor. Can we have tile 316, please? I think you made a note of what you saw the second time you saw [Baby O].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So this is timed at 7 o'clock, but again would that be written in retrospect when the opportunity arose?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Neonatal consultant gave an update. Dr Rackham agreed with..."?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That's "management".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "... so far"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And, "Advised to try for..."?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: "Central access."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We have heard about UVC and UAC:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "He agreed to get an update for [is that] bed state for transfers"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, "transfer and call back".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You returned to the resuscitation and again you've put:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "For details and times, refer to Dr Brearey's notes and chart."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So just from recollection, do you recall what was unfolding when you went back to the nursery?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. I think he'd probably done the same thing. So I remember going in and the resuscitation rounds of adrenaline and bicarb being done again.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You say again. Had there been an improvement in [Baby O]'s condition before you left?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So between the time -- so when I said -- when [Dr A], Dr Brearey and myself were there after the re-intubation and that episode of desaturation and bradycardia, we'd put him back on the ventilator and he appeared to be stable, if you can use the word, which was why I thought: well, okay, we've got this moment now, let's sort of go back and have a re-think, we've
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: considered different things and let's run it past another consultant.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. When you came back things had deteriorated again?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What was happening when you came back?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So he was receiving doses of adrenaline every 4 minutes and we also gave him some bicarbonate. During this time we had also thought about could he have a pneumothorax, so we cold -used a cold light to check for that because we couldn't really understand why these collapses and crashes were happening. It's not something I'd seen happen so suddenly in a baby, literally so quickly one after another. It just seemed like whatever we gave him was having no effect.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. With the resuscitation process being the protocol that it seems to be, would you have expected a response from the measures that were being taken?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: In the first place, I couldn't explain why he had crashed in the first place. Generally speaking, if...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm trying to answer this as best as I can. So normally, if you revive a baby with ventilating them and supporting their breathing and their circulation with fluids, trying to improve their perfusion with dopamine, the answer is, yes, I would have expected a response from the medication that he was receiving.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Before you'd gone to speak to Dr Rackham, you'd seen that improvement?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So that was the third time or the second time. He did that once and then [Dr A] intubated him. Then he went again. Then we re-intubated him. Then he went again and then he had stabilised three times and this was the fourth time.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You mentioned a cold light test. We know that's only an indicative test, but what did that show or not show?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: The cold light test is to check for -- so we are going through different --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, we've had this evidence and it's not been challenged.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Sorry. What was the result of the cold light test (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: It was negative. The cold light is to check for a big air leak that can compromise a baby suddenly and might be one explanation --
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Was there any evidence on the cold light test?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Was at one point an intraosseous route sought?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So when we were trying to get a capillary gas -- so the venous cannulation did not give us the blood test, the heel pricks weren't giving us any blood, and we wanted to know the blood gas. So the blood gas gives us quite a lot of information about the oxygenation, perfusion and guides on what other resuscitative measures may be helpful. So Dr Gibbs was there and he used an intraosseous needle, which is --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We have heard that's a needle into the shinbone, in this case, to obtain blood from within the bone.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just to be clear, the purpose of the intraosseous needle was what, to obtain what?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: To get some blood because there was no other way we could get any blood from him.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At the time that was undertaken you have told us there were two intravenous points of access. Were they still operable?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And was there, at another point, an attempt to reduce the distension of [Baby O]'s stomach by use of a -- entry via the McBurney's point, we've heard it called?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. These are now, we are trying to think -- one of the differentials was his abdomen was grossly distended and we know that when there is a lot of air or gas in the abdomen it pushes the diaphragm up and that compromises the breathing and can compromise the heart.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So another was, well, if we reduce this abdominal distension, will that help? So Dr Brearey then took a cannula and inserted to see if there was a massive air leak or if the bowel had perforated and all the air had leaked out and that had distended the abdomen to the point that it was compromising his
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: cardiovascular status. And he inserted the little yellow cannula lower down on the right side of the abdomen.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did it relieve the distension?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: No. He just got a little bit of blood that was -- there was nothing.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And did the attempts to resuscitate by way of adrenaline and chest compressions continue?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: We did however many rounds, I think there were four or six. There was a period of time, again, that I've documented in my statement, when he was again stabilised a little bit and there was a discussion about baptising him and whilst he was being baptised he became severely bradycardic again and resuscitation attempts were commenced yet again and I think he received another four rounds or however many from, I think, 5.15 until 5.45.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Scroll down to the rest of the note, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You spoke to both parents regarding what was unfolding?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You remember them being present?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I don't.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You've noted there the use of the intraosseous needle —
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- and Dr Gibbs, and the further adrenaline, which sadly had no effect. Is that a note to say that resuscitation was discontinued at 17.47?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Your final note on the page is the leaving of a message with contact details with the coroner's office; do you recall doing that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: No, I don't.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you remember attempting to contact the coroner's office the following day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I don't. I got a call from -- I remember speaking to somebody in that same room. I don't think I contacted them, I think they called back, so I must have had the message to call them back.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Again, it's documented in there, but I do remember going in there and speaking to someone the following day.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did anything unusual happen while you were on the phone to the coroner?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: The following day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I think it did. Again, I haven't gone through that statement in detail.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You're going to come and give evidence separately about [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just to conclude your evidence with regard to [Baby O], what was it that happened when you first tried to speak to the coroner the following day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I haven't gone through [Baby P]'s notes in detail and I don't want to say the wrong thing, but I... [Baby P] again crashed that many times, I don't know whether one of those was when I was speaking to him.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. All right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: But I would need to check my notes on that.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can maybe return to that when you come back to tell us about [Baby P].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Could we finish, please, with tile 477, just for the sake of completeness? We can see there two notes in that regard. At 7.30 pm, so a couple of hours after [Baby O] had passed, you spoke to his parents about a coroner's post-mortem. It's at 2.25 and you have recorded speaking to someone called Chris from the coroner's office and providing the relevant details.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you. [Dr B], I have no more questions.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If you could wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
[Dr B], just a couple of points, if I may, just with regard to how [Baby O] looked when you first saw him.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'm going to go to the first of the notes that we have, the clinical note. It's at tile 218. This is a note that you made in retrospect, [Dr B], at 6.15 pm.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I know you are casting your mind back now and you began by trying to recall things as well as you could before you had the notes and you described that when you came back to see [Baby O] after the bleep had gone off and you were with Dr Brearey, you made reference to him looking mottled, is the way you put it.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Are we talking about the initial 3 pm note or...?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I'm just looking first of all at this one.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we look here, from 3.50, which is when you first went back with [Dr A] --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: [Dr A]? You said Dr Brearey.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: My mistake, with [Dr A]. 3.50. You said you'd gone back with [Dr A] and [Baby O] was being bagged --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- and he was generally mottled.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we look at the note here, you can probably read it yourself, but it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Written retrospectively from 3.50. Was with [Dr A] who was updating me about [Baby O]'s condition, had been intubated at 3 pm."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You recite that:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Arrived to find [Baby O] was being bagged."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And you move on then and there's never any reference to him being mottled?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: No, there isn't.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We looked at a later note that you made later on.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We can go to it if you want to but it was at tile 316.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A few hours later and again no reference to any mottling then.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just to cut through all of this, I have looked in the your statement as well to the police, which is dated 22 November 2017, and you go into quite a lot of detail there but there's no description about mottling there either. I'm just wondering whether, doing the best you can, mottling is something that appears but might not have been there at the time, appeared in your recollection but might not have been there at the time.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Okay. So I will expand on that a little bit. Mottling is a general term that is used when babies are very poorly perfused. Okay?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: So when the circulation becomes poor, the supply -- the body tries to preserve the blood supply to the vital organs and takes it away from the skin, which is not a vital organ, and that leads to mottling.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: It is a sign of very poor circulation. While I have not mentioned the word "mottling", I think there is enough evidence there, by not being able to bleed a baby after stabbing them several times, to show that their circulation was very, very poor. So I think when I say mottling, it's the poor circulation, so one of the things that sticks in your mind is, well, the circulation is -- this baby is having a circulatory collapse.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That explains it, I just wanted to be clear when you were saying mottling exactly what you were referring to.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It has a significance here and you have explained that, poor perfusion, which is what you'd expect of a baby in circumstances like this. You're nodding. You're agreeing, I take it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, sorry. Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The other matter I'd be grateful if you'd help with is this. We know that the actual process of CPR was performed on [Baby O] on two separate occasions that afternoon. I'm going to ask Mr Murphy to put up tile 227, which is a document that records when it took place.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We know from the note that you made that we've just looked at, [Dr B], that you'd recalled that external compressions commenced at 16.30. That's your approximate recollection. We can see, if you look on this chart, that we've got, "Chest compressions started" -- do you see it says 16.19? If you look at where it says "chest compressions started" at the top?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And it's got a record there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm not raising any point about the fact it says 4.30 in your note and 4.19 here, that's not the point of my question. But I just wanted to ask if you could help us with how long that went on for, if you have any recollection of that particular session of chest compressions?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: All I will say to you is when people who are directly involved in the resuscitation are not -- so there is a person assigned to time and document. And the start and stop times, however precise they can be, are documented by that person. So once you've got a scriber assigned, my timings might not have been precise because that wasn't my job. But I couldn't say to you exactly how long. However, within a few minutes, his circulation did return, his heart rate was re-established, and he was -- we did manage to connect him back to the ventilator and that would have only happened after some degree of stabilisation had occurred.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So maybe a matter of minutes, but you couldn't say how many?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: DR B: No.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm not going to ask you to guess then. I just wondered if it was something you could remember. That's all I wanted to ask. Thank you, [Dr B].
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I have nothing, my Lord. Does my Lord have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You will be required to give evidence again, [Dr B], but thank you very much for coming to give evidence this afternoon. Please don't talk to anyone about anything to do with this case until it's finished.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. Remain where you are, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think there were -- I don't know who was going to be reading statements. Will there be any difficulty in -- rather than the disruption of the jury leaving the court and the witness leaving the court, would there be in difficulty in your remaining here for the 5 or 10 minutes it'll take to read these?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It might take a little longer, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Will it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I'm fine with waiting.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Are you sure? Is there any difficulty about anything being said in any of these statements that should not be heard by the witness? In other words, it might be prejudicial or corrupt your recollections or something.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm just looking at the statements I've got. Most of them are scored through.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. There's three nurses and two doctors left. Fairly short statements. I'll do them as quickly as I can.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was trying to save a bit of time, but I'm wasting it by conducting this exercise. So we'll just carry on. Are you all right with that?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS SAMANTHA O'BRIEN (read)
My Lord, the next statement is Samantha O'Brien, who appears at page 51 of my Lord's bundle. She in a statement dated 10 May 2018 says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Between January 2016 and July 2017 I worked as a band 5 nurse within the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital in Cheshire.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I confirm that I was designated nurse for [Baby O] during my long day shift on 22 June 2016. [Baby O] was in nursery 1 along
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: with one of his brothers, but I can't be certain whether he was with [Baby P] or [Baby R].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "During my shift [Baby O] was progressing well and there were no issues."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, I'm not going to go to it, but if anyone wants the note of that day shift it appears behind tile 48 in our sequence.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She adds:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I also believe I was designated nurse for [Baby R] that day.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The following day, 23 June 2016, I was working a long day shift on the neonatal unit and I was the designated nurse for [Baby R]. Lucy Letby and her student nurse, Rebecca Morgan, were the designated nurses for [Baby R]'s brothers, [Baby P] and [Baby O].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I recall all three triplets being in nursery 2 at the start of the shift. I was not continuously in nursery 2 as I believe I was also allocated a baby in another of the rooms. As nursery 2 is not intensive care, there is no requirement to remain in the room and the unit is small enough to hear if the alarms activate.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I recall, as I entered nursery 2, that [Baby P] and [Baby R]'s incubators were on the right side of the room and [Baby O]'s cot was on the left side by the window. I don't recall there being any issues raised in relation to any of the triplets during the morning handover.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At some point during the afternoon, I can't be more specific, I recall that Lucy had requested a review of [Baby O] by the doctor. From curiosity, I asked Lucy her reason for this and she explained that [Baby O] had blew his tummy up. I could see [Baby O] but other than his stomach may have appeared slightly distended, there was nothing else that was visibly apparent to me.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was outside of nursery 2 when I saw that [Baby O]'s incubator was transferred to nursery 1. I am unsure of the staff who moved [Baby O] but confirm it would have been two nurses.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was at this point I glanced at [Baby O] and saw that his skin appeared a bluey colour. I'm aware this is symptomatic of desaturation in babies. I knew that [Baby O] was placed on a ventilator and stabilised. I recall the triplets' parents being
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: on the ward at this point and I took them into nursery 2 where they had cuddles with [Baby R].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was aware that my colleagues were focusing on nursery 1 and I was either spoken to discreetly or I went into nursery 1 to see what was happening. It was at this time that the parents were informed that [Baby O] had deteriorated and they were taken into nursery 1. I then assisted in drawing up the drugs required in [Baby O]'s resuscitation procedure. I was working alongside Yvonne Farmer while drawing the drugs up and when she left I was later assisted by Melanie Taylor.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Sadly, [Baby O] continued to deteriorate and he tragically passed away. I am aware that he was baptised but I have no further recollection of this taking place.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I had no involvement in the aftercare with the [Family of Babies O, P & R]. I did attend a debrief which was led by Dr Brearey and took place during the same shift."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS YVONNE GRIFFITHS (read)
The next statement, please, my Lord, is from Yvonne Griffiths and appears at page 54 in the bundle.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is dated 26 March 2018 and she says as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am currently employed as the ward manager at the Countess of Chester Hospital in Cheshire. I have been asked to provide any information I can offer in relation to a set of triplets born on 21 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I confirm that I was on duty on 23 June 2016. I was officebased that day but obviously if my colleagues on the unit needed assistance, then I would support them. 23 June was the only date that I worked during the specific period involving the [Surname of Babies O, P & R] triplets.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The triplets, [Baby O], [Baby P] and [Baby R], were in nursery 2 and were stable at that time, with Lucy Letby being the designated nurse for [Baby O] and [Baby P]. Lucy also had a student working with her as well and I believe that Rebecca Morgan was allocated the care of [Baby R] that shift.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The [Surname of Babies O, P & R] triplets were classed as IT because they had lines in and possibly oxygen. [Baby O]'s cot was positioned first on the right as you entered the room and he was the baby we transferred into nursery 1 when he started to deteriorate. We only have one emergency admission space that we can transfer a baby into and as we were busy with patients, we
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: did have to move a baby from nursery 1 to allow [Baby O] space in the room.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When [Baby O] was in nursery 1, his cot was opposite the door. The medication cupboard that's used for resuscitation procedures is kept in nursery 1 and the drugs have to be checked by two members of staff.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember being alerted to [Baby O]'s collapse as I was walking through the unit and I could see a lot of activity in nursery 2. I saw the staff were focused around [Baby O].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We were very busy at that time so we moved the more stable baby out of nursery 1 and transferred [Baby O] to nursery 1. My only involvement at this time was to assist with moving equipment and ventilators.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "All the medical/nursing team were involved with [Baby O] and I recall [Baby O]'s father who was also present and looking very distraught. My role at that point was to support the father as there were enough people present to draw up the medication. Sometimes too many people can be more of a hazard in that situation.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember supporting and holding the father's hand and discussing things with him as he was witnessing everything that was happening at the time with [Baby O]. I know [Mother of Babies O, P & R] was also on the ward, but I don't recall her being in a wheelchair, I also remember [Mother of Babies O, P & R]'s mother being around.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Dr Gibbs and Dr Brearey were also present with [Dr B], who spoke with the parents. It was unusual to have the three consultants present at the same time. Unfortunately, when [Baby O] did die, the nurses were very busy caring for other babies on the ward, so I took the parents into the family room and sat with them with [Baby O] in his cot.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remained with the family for quite a long time that day. My duty that shift ended at 5 pm but I stayed until the night staff came on duty and handed over the care to them as, in a situation like that, I did not want to just leave.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby O] was later taken through to nursery 2 to be with his brothers and family and we ensured they were the only babies present in that room at that time to respect the parents' privacy."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That concludes her statement, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR JOHN GIBBS (read)
The next statement comes from Dr Gibbs and it begins at page 63 of my Lord's bundle.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Gibbs, in a statement dated 10 September 2018, says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby O] was the second of three triplets born on 21 June 2016 at 33 weeks' gestation. He was born under the care of one of my consultant colleagues, [Dr B]. I had no involvement with his care until the evening of 23 June 2016 when I was the consultant on call for that evening and night covering the neonatal unit and paediatric ward.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I went to the neonatal unit at around 17.00 hours on 23 June 2016. I cannot recall exactly what time I went to the unit, nor is this recorded in [Baby O]'s hospital record. When I arrived on the neonatal unit, [Baby O] was extremely ill and was receiving cardiorespiratory resuscitation directed by two of my consultant colleagues, [Dr B] and Dr Steve Brearey. Other junior doctors were involved as well as a number of the nurses on the neonatal unit but I cannot recall exactly who else was involved at that time.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I had only peripheral involvement since the resuscitation was already underway when I arrived on the neonatal unit and this was being led by [Dr B] and Dr Brearey. These two colleagues, plus nurses and junior doctors, recorded their involvement in [Baby O]'s medical record but there was no need for me to make an entry in that record since I did not have a significant involvement with [Baby O]. Instead, as the consultant on call for the neonatal unit that evening, I directed my attention to [Baby O]'s triplet siblings, [Baby P] and [Baby R]."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: In respect of [Baby O], my Lord, that concludes Dr Gibbs' statement.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR SUDESHNA BHOWMIK (read)
If I can move next, please to, Dr Bhowmik at page 67. Dr Bhowmik says this in a statement dated 4 January 2018:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am currently employed as a consultant paediatrician at Arrowe Park Hospital. From March 2016 through to September 2016, I was working as an ST8 registrar within the paediatric department at the Countess of Chester Hospital. This was my final year as a trainee before qualifying as a consultant.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On 23 June 2016, I was on call and working a long day shift and had worked within the children's ward. At 16.30 to 17.00 we had the usual handover and I recall the on-call consultant, Dr John Gibbs, was also present but unusually no one representing the neonatal unit had arrived. We made our way across to the unit and entered the intensive care room (room 1) to find the resuscitation of baby [Baby O] taking place.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "From referring to the medical notes, [Dr A], consultant [Dr B], consultant Dr Stephen Brearey and Dr Kath Cooke were present. There were also nurses around the baby but I do not remember who.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We had arrived towards the end of the resuscitation attempt and I took over from [Dr A] and conducted the last series of cardiac compressions before, sadly, death was pronounced. Dr Gibbs and I immediately examined the other two siblings who were in the HDU room (room 2). As a preventative measure, samples of bloods were sent to the laboratory to look for infection markers and both babies were placed on antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We had no concerns for either of the siblings at this time and I had no further involvement within the neonatal unit for the remainder of this shift."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of MR CHRISTOPHER BOOTH (read)
My Lord, next, please, is Christopher Booth.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: In a statement dated 15 March 2018, he says:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked to provide any information in relation to my involvement with a set of triplets born on 21 June 2016 at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On Thursday, 23 June 2016, I was working on a long day shift, beginning with the handover at 07.30 hours that morning. I believe that on this day [Baby O] was in nursery 1, however I am only surmising this as the triplets were quite new admissions and usually triplets on day 1 or day 2 would be placed in nursery 1. This room is the main admission and intensive care nursery. I know that [Baby P] and [Baby R] went into nursery 2 at some point but I cannot confirm which day."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: He then confirms that the map that, my Lord, is in jury bundle 1 is an accurate representation of the unit.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't think I need to refer to that again for now.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "I can't confirm the position of [Baby O]'s cot in nursery 1 and cannot recall whether I was a designated nurse for any of the triplets on 23 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Sadly that day, [Baby O] had some abdominal distension and he rapidly deteriorated and later suffered a cardiac arrest. My only involvement with [Baby O]'s care was during his resuscitation procedure whereby I was working in a supportive role and checking drugs.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It is standard practice that two registered nurses check the drugs as some of the drugs we administer are quite complex and not straightforward. The drug volume provided is calculated against the baby's weight. However, I don't specifically recall who I checked the drugs with during this situation.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I cannot recall whether I had any contact with the [Family of Babies O, P & R] after [Baby O] sadly passed away. When it became apparent that [Baby O] was not going to survive, the mood among staff was understandably sombre and we were all shocked and disappointed.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby O] had looked like a triplet that potentially was going to sail through. He was a good size and not even that premature. It was so unexpected that he just suddenly collapsed with no indication that would happen and so it caught us all by surprise.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "As a precaution both [Baby P] and [Baby R] were placed nil by mouth with a possible cause being sepsis and they were both commenced on antibiotics and put on to drips. [Baby P] and [Baby R] were both okay overnight."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That concludes insofar as [Baby O] is concerned Nurse Booth's statement.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, there's one more statement to read, but that can be done in the morning.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Certainly. I don't want to cause any difficulty. It's 3 o'clock then, members of the jury.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We'll break off there. It's almost all that was going to be dealt with today in any event. That's it for today. 10.30 tomorrow morning. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Please remember your responsibilities as jurors. No communication with anyone by any means about anything to do with this case other than when you are all together and any communications that you have between you should be confined to what I call administrative matters, nothing to do with the case
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: itself or any of the evidence in the case, I'm sure you understand what I'm talking about. So by all means communicate but nothing to do with the evidence in this case unless you're all together and can hear what the others are saying.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
We'd be grateful if we could have a visit with Ms Letby, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: If you just wait there, please, [Dr B] and the rest of the court will go. Perhaps some of the lawyers may still be lingering but you'll be told when you may leave the court.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR B: Okay, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The court adjourned until 10.30 am on Wednesday, 15 March 2023)
